summary: This page from the American Soybean Association describes the Soy Ink Seal program. It explains that soy ink is made from soybeans, is more environmentally friendly than petroleum-based ink, and its history began with the Newspaper Association of America in the late 1970s. It also lists minimum soybean oil content standards for different ink types and outlines how license royalty payments and renewals work.
one_line: The American Soybean Association's Soy Ink Seal page covering soy ink history, minimum soy oil standards, and licensing and royalty terms.
key_facts: Soy ink is made from soybeans and is accepted as more environmentally friendly than traditional petroleum-based ink.
Soy-based ink is slower to dry than many inks but provides more accurate colors and makes it easier to recycle paper.
In the late 1970s, the Newspaper Association of America (NAA) sought new ink methods due to rising petroleum prices and quarrels with OPEC countries.
After testing more than 2,000 vegetable oil formulations, NAA researchers settled on soybean oil.
In 1987, soybeans were successfully tested by The Gazette from Iowa in a practical printing run.
Today about one-third of America's nearly 10,000 newspaper printers use soy ink.
More than 90% of the nation's daily newspapers are printed with color soy ink.
Soy inks allow a reduction in ink coverage by 85% compared to water-based inks for label printing.
Black news ink requires 40% soy oil content by formula weight under the SoySeal minimum standards.
Heat-set ink requires 7% soy oil content, and UV/EB ink also requires 7%.
Soy Ink License Agreements renew annually on January 1, and royalty payments during the year are pro-rated by quarter.
All license payments are in U.S. Dollars.
After payment is received, ASA emails a soy ink or soy oil logo and a signed certified contract within 72 hours.
Questions about license payments may be directed to Sharetha Newsome at snewsome@soy.org.
